title: Cold Lake First Nations seeking judicial review of Pacific Link pipeline designation
summary: Cold Lake First Nations filed an application Thursday for judicial review in Federal Court, challenging Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest.

image.caption: Cold Lake First Nations is seeking judicial review of a pipeline designation. Chief Kelsey Jacko is shown here speaking during the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) 2026 Annual General Assembly in Ottawa in July. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Cold Lake First Nations filed an application Thursday for judicial review in Federal Court, challenging Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest.
West Coast pipeline set to be fast-tracked under the Building Canada Act
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 08, 2026 3:37 PM EDT | Last Updated: 9 hours ago

Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday, challenging Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced last week the pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia would be fast-tracked under the Building Canada Act. The goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year, so construction can begin next September.

Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko previously said his community was left out of consultations on the pipeline designation, despite the fact that his community is situated in the oilsands region.

"They've been consulting all these nations around us, there's over 120 nations that have been consulted and we've been left out of the talks," said Chief Kelsey Jacko in an interview with CBC earlier this week, before the application was filed.

"All the oil comes from my traditional territories, but yet we're left out of the equity talks. It's very troublesome," said Jacko, referring to Prime Minister Mark Carney's promise that Indigenous communities would be offered at least a 10 per cent ownership stake in Pacific Link.

Carney also mentioned the Pathways Project, a carbon capture and storage initiative, which would absorb millions of tonnes of carbon emissions annually and store them underground, as he announced that Pacific Link would a project of national interest.
Jacko said he worries that may mean waste could be stored under his land.

"We have repeatedly tried to work with Canada on both the Pacific Link and Pathways, and Canada has gone ahead with the decision to designate Pacific Link as a project of national interest without meaningful consultation with First Nations," he said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Privy Council Office said while Pacific Link and the Pathways project were linked through agreements between Alberta and Canada, they are still two distinct projects with separate proponents, regulatory processes and decision-making projects.

"Currently, responsibility for Indigenous consultation and engagement on the Pathways Project rests with the provincial authorities overseeing its review and approval processes," said the spokesperson.
In the application for judicial review, Cold Lake First Nations' lawyers said the designation breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown.

blocks.text: "Increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects on the ability of CLFN members to maintain their Luechogh Tue Denesuline way of life as promised by Treaty No. 6," the application said.
"Canada has made no effort to understand or mitigate the massive cumulative effects of oilsands development on CLFN's Luechogn Tue Denesuline treaty rights."

items: West Coast oil pipeline becomes 1st project designated in national interest

blocks.text: The First Nation is asking the court to quash the national interest designation and to declare that Canada has a duty to consult with the community on the pipeline.

The Assembly of First Nations previously told The Canadian Press it had identified "many red flags" in the pipeline's national interest designation and says the federal government appears to be predetermining outcomes and approving projects in advance of meaningful consultations.
Carney promised his major projects agenda would not interfere with Canada's obligations under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
With files from Jennifer Yoon
